events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Noah proposes Noah, Felix. I know I am Good; Felix is an untested choice for the second spot.

I have no objection to Noah and Felix. My reasoning is simple: mission one is a two-person team, so the leader's first pick going to himself is reasonable, and picking an untested player rather than the two players who were floated is not something I can criticize on paper alone. My only soft preference is that across the five missions we rotate so everyone, including me, gets at least one outing. If Felix has a read on the table after this mission, I would much rather have us pull information from every seat than let the same two names run again and again. Nothing in what I have seen so far argues for rejecting this team, and a rejected team costs us an attempt with only one failure remaining before Evil takes the game. So my vote is to approve Noah and Felix and move on. If anyone wants to make the case for a different second name, make it now and make it with reasons, not vibes.

I support this team proposal. Speaking for myself, I know 100% that I am Good and will play a Success on this mission. From my perspective, having myself on the team ensures at least half the team is confirmed Good to me, making this a great test of Noah. Since this is Mission 1, getting an early mission underway gives the table clean data to evaluate going forward. Unless anyone has a compelling reason against it, I am ready to vote Approve.

I mostly agree with what Zara laid out. Mission one is about generating clean information, and a rejected team here burns one of our only two attempts, so the bar for switching names should be high. I take Felix's self-vouching the way I take anyone's self-vouching on this game — everyone at this table can say they are Good, so it moves nothing for me either way. What does move me is the rotation point. If Noah and Felix run mission one and it succeeds, the natural instinct next round will be to reward them with another outing, and suddenly two seats have played twice while the rest of us have played once. That compresses the information we get across five missions. I am not asking Noah to change the team. I would just like to hear, before we vote, whether he already has a rotation plan in mind for missions two and three, or whether he is picking purely on instinct this round. My vote is leaning approve either way, but the answer shapes how I read his later proposals.

Kenji, I picked Felix on instinct; I don't have a fixed rotation plan. A successful mission would be useful evidence, but it wouldn't prove both of us are Good, since Evil can play Success. For later teams, I'll weigh mission results and votes rather than rotate automatically. Also, a rejection here wouldn't leave only one attempt: Evil wins after five rejected teams on the same mission. I still favor keeping Noah and Felix.

I approve Noah and Felix, and my approval has not changed. Let me add one thing to Kenji's rotation point, because I think it cuts in the other direction from the one he framed. Noah is right that a mission success is not proof — a two-person team can pass with one Evil Fail card alongside one Success. So mission results alone will never tell us who is who. The real information in this game comes from how people talk: who proposes, who volunteers, who deflects, and how consistently a player's stated reasoning holds up when a proposal is actually put in front of them. That is why I want the table spread across seats rather than clustering around one or two comfortable names.

So my soft preference for later missions is stronger than a simple rotation rule: I would like every proposal to involve a mix — at least one player who has already been tested and at least one who has not — and I would like to hear from players who have not yet spoken on a proposal before the vote, not only from the two people who would be on it. A player who never talks is a player we learn nothing about, and after three successful missions the game ends with an assassination phase where guessing wrong on Merlin loses everything. We need data on more than two people, and we get it fastest by putting new names on the table early, while a rejection still costs us little.

On this proposal itself: Felix's self-vouching is worth exactly as much as anyone's, and no more. Noah selecting himself is standard and reasonable on a two-person team. There is no evidence in front of the table that either name is a worse bet than the alternative, and with only one failure before Evil takes three, a rejected team here is an expensive way to buy very little. I vote Approve.

One request for the record, not as a challenge to the team: before we vote, I would like Felix to say plainly what evidence he would want before he agrees to another team with the same two names, and I would like Noah to tell us whether his picks for mission two will be chosen by what he learned here or by who he most wants to sit beside. That is not a demand for a change to this team. It is a request that we start evaluating proposals on reasons we can compare rather than instinct.

I support the proposed team of Noah and Felix. On mission one, with no concrete evidence against either name, rejecting the leader’s first proposal would spend one of our limited attempts for very little gain. Noah choosing himself is standard for a two-person team, and Felix has committed publicly to playing Success. I agree with Zara that mission results alone will not prove alignment, so what matters is the discussion record. I would also like future proposals to spread information across more seats, but that is a reason to evaluate later teams carefully, not to reject this one without cause. I will vote Approve.

To address Zara's question: if Mission 1 succeeds, it will be a positive sign, but I recognize an Evil player could play Success on a two-person mission to gain cover. For future missions—like Mission 2, which requires three players—I would not support blindly locking in the same core without scrutiny. I would want to look closely at the voting patterns on this proposal, how players reacted to the discussion, and incorporate fresh players to widen our information pool rather than creating an unvetted clique. Everyone at the table seems prepared to approve this proposal to establish our first benchmark, and I remain fully ready to vote Approve.

Zara, my later picks will depend on the mission result, votes, and discussion, not simply on who I want beside me. One correction: a team with one Fail card fails this mission; a success could still include Evil choosing Success. I remain in favor of Noah and Felix.

I approve Noah and Felix, and I want to be plain that my approval is a considered one rather than a default.

On the merits of this proposal: it is a two-person team on mission one, Noah is the leader and included himself, which is the least interesting possible choice, and Felix volunteered a public commitment to Success. Nobody has put forward a single fact that makes either of them a worse bet than the alternatives available to Noah, which were Zara, Kenji, and Amara. With only one failed mission tolerated before Evil takes the game, spending an attempt to substitute one untested name for another untested name would be paying a real price for information we cannot yet name. Felix's own point is the right one: a two-person team can succeed with an Evil Success card, so what we learn from mission one is not alignment, it is the shape of each player's reasoning and the consistency between what they say and what they do.

Where I want to push the table forward is on how we read later proposals. My preference is that each future team contain at least one player we have already seen behave under scrutiny, so that we can compare a fresh name against a known reference point rather than judging every new player in isolation with no baseline. That is a preference about the quality of our evidence, not a demand that any particular seat be excluded.

Amara, I would like to ask you one specific thing, since your contribution so far has been a general statement of support rather than a stated standard. What is the evidence threshold you are applying? You wrote that there is "no concrete evidence against either name" and that rejecting would spend an attempt for very little gain. Concretely: what would you have needed to see, before this vote, in order to have voted against Noah and Felix, and what will you be looking for in a proposal for mission two that would make you vote no? I ask because I want to know whether your approvals are being generated by evidence or by a general preference for moving the game along, and I would rather learn that now, from you, than infer it later from a vote.

Everyone else, my vote is Approve for Noah and Felix. Bring me reasons, not vibes, for later teams.

Zara, to answer your question directly: my threshold for voting against Noah and Felix before this vote would have been a concrete inconsistency or specific adverse signal, not merely the fact that another untested name was available. For example, a contradiction between what a nominee said and what they did, a refusal to answer a relevant direct question, or a stated reason that did not match the proposal would have moved me to no. I do not treat “no evidence against” as proof of Good; I treat it as insufficient reason to spend a rejection on mission one when the discussion itself has produced a usable record. Felix has now answered your question about future teams by saying he would scrutinize voting patterns and widen the pool, and Noah has clarified both his selection basis and the rejection rule. Those answers are consistent enough for me to keep my Approve on Noah and Felix. For mission two, I will vote no if the leader cannot explain how the proposal reflects the mission result, the public votes, or the discussion record; if a proposed player has dodged scrutiny or given inconsistent reasoning; or if the team appears chosen for comfort rather than evidence. I will also weigh whether the proposal gives us comparable information across seats, as you asked. On this team, I still see no concrete adverse evidence, so I support it.

Nothing in this discussion has changed my view, so I will keep this brief. I am voting Approve on Noah and Felix. The case for the team is the same one I laid out earlier: mission one exists to generate a clean benchmark, a rejection here spends an attempt on an untested name for another untested name, and both Noah and Felix have answered every question put to them without hedging. Noah's correction on the rejection rules was accurate, and his explanation that later picks will be driven by results, votes, and the discussion record rather than habit was exactly the standard I hoped he would articulate. Felix's answer about Mission 2 was also constructive — he explicitly declined to lock in the same core and committed to scrutinizing voting patterns and widening the pool. That is the right posture, and I will hold him to it when the three-person proposal comes. Amara's statement of her evidence threshold was clear and specific enough that I have no follow-up on it: inconsistency, dodged scrutiny, or comfort-based selection would move her to no, and I find that a reasonable standard that I share. My one closing note for the record is about interpretation, not this vote. If this mission succeeds, the result tells us very little about alignment, since an Evil player can play Success for cover on a two-person team. What will actually be informative is the vote pattern we are about to produce and whether everyone's stated standards here match their behavior on the next proposal. I will be watching specifically for whether the players who asked for evidence-based selection apply that standard themselves when they hold or influence leadership. With that said, this is a low-risk team with no adverse signals, and I see no reason to burn an attempt. I am ready to vote Approve.
Noah confirms Noah, Felix. I am keeping Noah and Felix; discussion revealed no compelling reason to substitute another untested player.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Noah, Felix. I am proposing myself, Noah, and Felix. As leader I want three seats of information, and this is the only pairing that combines two players who have already behaved under scrutiny on Mission 1 with a third established seat. Mission 1's success proves nothing about alignment since a two-person team can pass with an Evil Success card, so the real evidence I am weighting is the discussion record: Felix publicly committed to Success, Noah corrected the rejection rule accurately and explained his selection basis, and both answered direct questions without hedging. Keeping the same core for a three-person Mission 2 also gives me a reference point to read the other two players against when their votes and reactions come in. The remaining names on the table have produced general statements of support rather than a stated standard, so I would rather not spend Mission 2 on seats I know least and come away with two new reads and no baseline. This is a deliberate choice of known-good reference points over breadth, and I am happy to rotate afterward.

I will vote Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix. Zara’s proposal meets the standard I stated earlier: she has explained how it reflects the Mission 1 discussion record rather than simple comfort. Mission 1’s success is weak evidence, but Noah and Felix both answered direct questions consistently, and Zara adds a new seat to that core, so the team includes both tested and untested information. My earlier concern was breadth, and I still want Mission 3 to bring in Kenji or me rather than automatically repeat this three-person core. But that is a reason to scrutinize the next proposal, not to reject this one now: with no adverse signal against any nominee, rejecting would burn an attempt and replace an explained choice with speculation. I will hold Zara to her own commitment to rotate afterward. Approve.

As leader I will keep Zara, Noah, Felix. Let me put my reasoning on the record in a form you can check later.

Mission 1 succeeded, but as Felix correctly noted, a two-person mission can pass with an Evil Success card, so the result is weak alignment evidence. What I am actually weighting is the discussion record, and there the two seats that have been under scrutiny performed well: Felix committed publicly to Success and answered the question about future teams with a specific standard (scrutinize voting patterns, widen the pool, do not lock in the same core without scrutiny). Noah corrected the rejection rule accurately, explained that later picks will be driven by results and discussion rather than habit, and answered directly. On the two-player mission every seat on this table produced a stated reason, not just a gesture of approval.

The other three names have produced, so far, statements of support without a falsifiable threshold. Amara came closest, naming inconsistency, dodged scrutiny, and comfort-based selection as her triggers, and I take that seriously. But I am not going to spend Mission 2 on the two seats I know least and end up with two new reads and no reference point. Reference points are how we make sense of new information. If Mission 3 brings in a fresh seat, I want it read against a known baseline, not in isolation.

So this is a deliberate trade: depth now, breadth on Mission 3. I am committing to that here so it can be held against me. My plan is that Mission 3, which needs two players, brings in Kenji or Amara alongside one of the seats we have now tested, and that Mission 4 and Mission 5 similarly put a fresh name on the table. If I propose the same three names again on Mission 3, treat that as a failure of my stated commitment and vote against me.

One specific question for Felix, since his Mission 2 answer is the commitment that most affects my plan: you said you would scrutinize voting patterns and incorporate fresh players rather than create an unvetted clique. Concretely, what evidence would you need on the table to support a Mission 3 team that contains one of the untested names, and what pattern in a proposal would make you vote no? I want to know in advance whether you are willing to widen the pool, because if you are not, my rotation plan and your stated standard are in conflict and I would rather discover that now than on the vote.

My own vote is Approve on Zara, Noah, Felix. I have no adverse evidence against any of them, and I am the one who put this team forward, so I accept responsibility for it.

Zara, to answer your question directly: I am entirely open to widening the pool on Mission 3, especially since Mission 3 requires only two players and Kenji will be the next leader. The evidence I would look for before approving an untested name comes down to consistency and how the table handles the Mission 2 outcome. If Mission 2 succeeds, Good reaches match point at 2-0. In that scenario, an untested player like Kenji proposing himself alongside someone vetted from the winning missions makes sense, provided his reasoning aligns with the discussion and voting record. If Mission 2 yields a Fail, the math shifts immediately: we know at least one Evil player is among you, Noah, or me, meaning Kenji and Amara cannot both be Evil in a five-player setup. In that case, bringing in an untested player becomes not just an option, but a mathematical necessity. What would cause me to vote no is any proposal that defies the hard information on the table—such as a player ignoring a Fail result, refusing to justify their selections, or proposing teams that shield unvetted combinations without sound deductive logic. As for the current proposal of Zara, Noah, and Felix: knowing my own Good alignment, this team gives me two-thirds visibility, and putting Zara under direct scrutiny alongside the Mission 1 participants is a sensible next step. I am ready to vote Approve.

I lean Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix: Mission 1 succeeded, and I know I am Good, though that result does not clear Felix. Zara is still untested, so this is not a known-Good team.

Zara, you said the remaining seats had only general statements of support, but Amara gave specific reasons she would reject a team, and Kenji endorsed those standards. How does that affect your comparison of them with Felix and me?

Also, Felix, knowing your own alignment gives you certainty about one of the three seats, not two-thirds of the team. We should avoid treating discussion or a successful mission as proof of alignment.

Answering Noah first, since he asked directly. Amara's standard is the most falsifiable thing on the table: inconsistency, dodged scrutiny, comfort-based selection. Kenji endorsed it explicitly. That matters to my comparison, and here is how it lands. I was not ranking Amara and Kenji below Felix and Noah because they said less. I ranked them by how they behaved under questioning. Felix and Noah were the two names on the table for three consecutive turns, both under direct questions about their selection basis and their rejection thresholds, and both answered with checkable commitments: Felix named the evidence he would want (voting patterns, consistency with the record, fresh names rather than a locked core), and Noah named his criteria (mission result, public votes, discussion record) and corrected the rejection rule accurately. Amara's threshold is precise and she has met it, but largely by stating it — she has not yet had to defend a selection she made under pressure, and neither has Kenji. That asymmetry is about exposure to scrutiny, not about who I find comfortable to sit with.

To Felix: your Mission 2 answer is the commitment that most affects my plan, and I want to sharpen one line in it. Saying that knowing your own alignment gives you "two-thirds visibility" on this team overstates it — your certainty clears exactly one seat, yourself. The other two have to be carried by the record, not by your role. I agree with your arithmetic on the Fail case; I would add that if this mission fails, this table learns a great deal immediately, and the next proposals should be read through that result rather than in spite of it.

I am keeping Zara, Noah, Felix, and I accept responsibility as leader for it. On my Mission 3 rotation commitment: I said a fresh seat beside a tested one, and I hold to it. But the leader of Mission 3 is Kenji, and I am not going to pretend I get to pick his team. My ask is the reverse of a challenge — it is a request for his criteria in advance.

Kenji, you lead Mission 3, so before this vote goes in: will you tell us the specific evidence you will cite for your two picks, and will you be including yourself? Not to fence you in — to give the table a standard to read your proposal against, which is exactly what I asked Amara for on Mission 1 and what she gave me. My vote is Approve.

Zara, you asked for my criteria for Mission 3 before this vote goes in, so let me answer directly rather than after the fact. I will be leading Mission 3, and my intention is to include myself alongside one player who has already been on a mission, exactly the tested-plus-fresh structure you asked for. My specific evidence for the second pick will come from two sources: the Mission 2 result and how the discussion and voting record lines up with what people committed to beforehand. If Mission 2 succeeds, I will weight consistency — whether the players who set standards here actually applied them. If Mission 2 fails, the arithmetic changes, as Felix laid out: at least one Evil would sit among Zara, Noah, and Felix, which means the fresh seat beside me becomes the most important information we can buy. So my pick will be driven by the result, not by comfort, and I am stating that now so you can hold me to it, which is the same courtesy Amara extended on Mission 1.

One clarification I would genuinely value from you, since your rotation commitment is the standard on the table: when you say Mission 3 should pair a fresh seat with a tested one, does a player who has voted and argued consistently but has not been on a mission — that is, me — count as tested in your framework, or does tested strictly mean mission-experienced? I ask because if I include myself as the fresh seat and pair myself with a mission veteran, I want to know whether that satisfies your commitment or whether you would read it as me stacking the team with unvetted names. Your answer shapes how I read your own vote on my proposal, so I would rather have it on the record now.

On the current proposal of Zara, Noah, and Felix: I am voting Approve. My reasoning is consistent with what I said on Mission 1. This team has no adverse signals — every member has answered direct questions without hedging, the leader explained her selection against the discussion record rather than habit, and she has put a falsifiable commitment in writing that we can vote against later if she breaks it. Zara, Noah, and Felix have all now been under some form of scrutiny, and nobody at this table has produced a specific inconsistency from any of them. Rejecting would burn an attempt to swap one explained choice for another, and I see nothing in the record that justifies that price. Felix's point about the Fail case is also correct and worth keeping in view: a failure here would be immediately informative, which cuts against panicking preemptively.

To Amara's earlier note: I share her expectation that Mission 4 and Mission 5 widen the pool further, and I will apply the same standard when I evaluate whoever holds leadership then. For now, my vote is Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix.

My vote is Approve on Zara, Noah, Felix, and I want my reasoning in a checkable form.

Answering Kenji directly, since he asked and the answer shapes how I read his Mission 3 proposal: I use "tested" in two layers. You have argued and voted under scrutiny twice now, so on the reasoning dimension I count you as tested; you have not yet been on a mission, so on the information dimension you are untested. My commitment was a fresh seat beside a mission-experienced one, and I read your plan of yourself plus one mission veteran as satisfying it, with you as the fresh seat by mission experience. I am endorsing that structure, not the name you pick for the veteran. I will want the reason for that name stated before the vote, as you promised, and if Mission 2 succeeds I will hold you to consistency rather than to comfort.

One point of record for everyone: I am not going to treat self-knowledge as evidence. Felix, your Mission 2 answer said that knowing your own alignment gives you "two-thirds visibility" on a three-person team. I only see one seat cleared by self-knowledge; the other two have to be carried by the record. That is a small correction on its own, but the pattern I want us to avoid is anchoring a team on seats nobody can cross-check. Nobody's certainty is verifiable by this table, mine included, so I will weigh the discussion record, the public votes, and whether stated standards are actually applied, and I will ask the rest of you to do the same.

Also worth putting on the record so nobody has to infer it: my Mission 3 plan is the one I already committed to, and I am stepping back from proposing it. Leadership should sit with whoever the rotation gives it, and the criteria for selection belong to the table rather than to me. I would rather be a reader of the record than the person who decides who sits on it.

And if this mission fails, at least one of the three of us is Evil, which means the two seats outside this team cannot both be Evil; the next proposals should be read through that result rather than around it.

Felix, one direct question and then I will stop: when you said knowing your own alignment gives you two-thirds visibility, how did you arrive at two-thirds, and what would you need to see on the table to treat a seat as cleared? I ask because I want to know whether your standard is one I can reuse when reading everyone else's claims.

Zara, to answer your question plainly: saying 'two-thirds visibility' was simply a slip of the tongue on the math. On Mission 1, being on a two-person team gave me one-half visibility (one out of two seats known). On this three-person team, knowing my own alignment gives me one-third certainty (one out of three seats), not two-thirds. Both you and Noah were entirely right to catch that.

As for what it takes to treat a seat as 'cleared': strictly speaking, for a Loyal Servant, no seat other than oneself can ever be 100% mathematically cleared until both Evil players are definitively identified elsewhere. Outside of that deduction, what I look for to treat a seat as trusted enough to approve is a consistent, falsifiable record. Specifically, that means proposing and supporting teams that match the hard game data rather than personal comfort, following through on stated commitments (such as your commitment to rotate on Mission 3), answering direct challenges without deflecting, and demonstrating deductive consistency between what a player says and how they vote.

Everyone at the table has engaged thoroughly, and Kenji has already outlined a clear, sound framework for Mission 3. I remain fully satisfied with this proposal and am ready to vote Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix.

This is my second and brief turn on Zara, Noah, and Felix. My vote is Approve, and the reasoning is unchanged from what I put on the record earlier: no adverse signal has been produced against any nominee across two full rounds of direct questioning, the leader has explained her selection against the discussion record rather than habit, and every member of this team has answered challenges without deflecting.

I want to acknowledge one thing for the record before we vote. Zara answered my question about the tested/untested distinction cleanly: I count as tested on the reasoning dimension and untested on the information dimension, and she endorsed a Mission 3 structure of one fresh seat beside one mission veteran, which is the plan I already committed to as the next leader. That exchange is exactly the kind of falsifiable, checkable standard I asked for, and it satisfies me that my own upcoming proposal will be read against a stated benchmark rather than vibes.

Felix's correction on the two-thirds slip was handled properly — he owned the arithmetic error and restated it correctly, which is itself a small positive data point on how he responds to being challenged. I note it without weighting it heavily either way; slips of the tongue happen, and what matters is whether the underlying reasoning was being stretched to justify a conclusion or simply misspoken. On the evidence available, it reads as the latter.

On the substance of the mission itself: if this succeeds, we sit at 2-0 and the information pressure shifts to consistency — whether the players who set standards here apply them when leadership rotates, which is what I will be watching as the next leader. If it fails, we learn that at least one Evil sits among these three, which means the two seats outside the team cannot both be Evil, and the arithmetic Felix and Zara both laid out takes over immediately. Either outcome is informative, and neither justifies burning a rejection to swap one explained choice for an unexplained one.

My final note is a commitment I want visible before the vote, since Zara has invited exactly this kind of accountability: as Mission 3 leader, I will propose myself plus one mission veteran, I will state my reason for the veteran pick before the vote rather than after, and if I fail to do either, I expect and invite votes against my proposal. That is the same standard I praised Amara for on Mission 1 and the same one Zara has applied to herself. Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix.

I have nothing new to add that changes the picture, so I will keep this short and put my closing position on the record. My vote is Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix.

Across two full rounds of discussion, every nominee on this team has answered direct questions without deflecting: Zara gave a falsifiable rotation commitment and answered my tested/untested question cleanly; Noah flagged the overstatement in the visibility framing rather than letting it stand; and Felix owned his arithmetic slip, restated it correctly, and laid out a concrete standard for what would move him to a no vote. Nobody at this table has produced a specific inconsistency against any of the three. The one weakness I might have cited — that this team repeats the Mission 1 core — has already been addressed head-on by the leader, who traded breadth now for breadth later and invited us to vote against her if she breaks that commitment. That is the kind of checkable reasoning I want to reward, not punish with a burned attempt.

I also want to restate my own commitment one final time before the vote, since accountability standards only mean something if they are held consistently. As Mission 3 leader I will propose myself plus one mission veteran, I will state my reason for the veteran pick before the vote rather than after, and if I fail on either count I expect votes against my proposal, starting with mine. I will hold the same standard for whoever leads Missions 4 and 5, including the expectation that fresh seats continue entering the pool.

Finally, on the interpretation point I raised earlier: whatever the result of this mission, the information that matters most is whether the standards stated in this discussion get applied when they are inconvenient. If this mission succeeds, we sit at 2-0 and the pressure shifts entirely to consistency of reasoning and voting. If it fails, we learn that at least one Evil sits among these three, which means the two seats outside the team cannot both be Evil, and every subsequent proposal should be read through that arithmetic. Either way, rejecting an explained team to substitute an unexplained one buys us nothing today. Approve on Zara, Noah, and Felix.

Zara confirms Zara, Noah, Felix. Keeping Zara, Noah, Felix. On the public record this is the strongest available read: both names on the team have been under direct questioning for two full rounds and have answered with checkable commitments rather than deflection, and Mission 1's success adds a weak but non-negative data point (a two-player success could have been an Evil Success, but it is still not adverse evidence). Against that, no nominee has produced any specific inconsistency, and a rejection would spend one of our two remaining attempts to swap one explained choice for another unexplained one, so the expected value of rejecting is poor. I also hold to the breadth commitment I made: this mission buys depth against known reference points, and I am committed to bringing a fresh seat onto Mission 3, which Kenji leads, and to widening the pool again on Missions 4 and 5. Voting Approve on Zara, Noah, Felix.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Noah. As committed on the record before this proposal: I am including myself as the fresh seat by mission experience, paired with one mission veteran. My pick for the veteran is Noah. Mission 1 succeeded with him on the team, and across two rounds of questioning he corrected the rejection rule accurately, stated his selection criteria plainly (mission result, public votes, discussion record rather than habit), and flagged the overstated visibility framing rather than letting it stand. That is exactly the consistency standard I said I would apply: if Mission 2 succeeds we sit at 2-0 and the pressure shifts to whether stated standards are applied, and Noah is the seat whose record most cleanly matches that test. Felix would also qualify, but Noah's correction of the rules detail is the most checkable data point on the table, so I weight it. This satisfies Zara's tested-plus-fresh structure with me as the fresh seat, and I state my reason before the vote as promised. If anyone believes a different veteran better fits the record, make the case now and I will weigh it before confirming.

I will vote Approve on Kenji and Noah, and I want to record why in a form that can be checked later.

Kenji's proposal matches the structure I endorsed before this vote: a fresh seat by mission experience beside a mission veteran, with the reason for the veteran stated before the vote rather than after. He named his reason, named the alternative he considered, and said why he weighted it lower. That is the standard I asked of him and he met it. Nothing in the record since Mission 1 has produced a specific inconsistency against either nominee, and rejecting an explained team here would spend one of our attempts to swap one explained choice for another. My vote is Approve.

Two things I want on the record for how we read the outcome.

First, I am not treating the Mission 1 and Mission 2 successes as evidence of alignment. Any two of those seats could have been one Evil playing Success next to a Good, so the results are weak data at best. I want both branches stated plainly so nobody reads the result through a prior expectation. If Mission 3 succeeds, we reach the assassination phase, and each of the five of us should assume the assassin is choosing among the three non-Evil seats, with no way for the rest of us to know which three those are. If it fails, then one of Kenji and Noah is the Fail card, and the arithmetic of the next proposal changes immediately.

Second, because the assassination phase is decided by how we talk rather than by how we vote, I want us to be deliberate about our public record. The tells an assassin looks for are the ones we have all been exhibiting: confident claims about our own alignment, quick corrections of other people's arithmetic, and analysis that runs a step ahead of the evidence. I am not pointing at anyone. Felix has been the most explicit about his own alignment, and I have been the one doing the most cross-referencing and correcting, and the standard I want us to apply is that all of those claims, mine most of all, should be discounted by the table and read as one Good player speaking rather than as proof of anything. Felix's stated standard for what it takes to treat a seat as cleared is the one I intend to use for the rest of this game, because it is the only one that points at the record rather than at a person's tone.

No new information from me, no corrections to offer, and nothing I want changed. Approve on Kenji and Noah.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
